unit.title: Comply with organizational requirements for protection and use of intellectual property

summary: This unit teaches you to comply with your organisation's requirements for the protection and use of intellectual property. You will learn the main types of IP and who owns them, how to follow the IP policy, how to use other people's material lawfully, how to protect your organisation's own ideas and confidential information, how to record and report new IP and breaches, and how to check compliance.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It teaches you to **comply with your organisation's requirements for the protection and use of intellectual property (IP)**: to know what IP is, to use other people's work lawfully, to protect your organisation's own ideas and confidential information, to record and report new IP, and to deal with breaches.

**Intellectual property** is the product of the mind: writing, designs, brands, software, music, images, recipes, inventions and business secrets. The law gives the owner rights over it, as it does over physical property. Every organisation uses other people's IP (software, fonts, music, photographs) and creates its own (training manuals, logos, product designs, client lists). Staff at every level can put their organisation at risk if they copy, share or publish without thinking.
**Who it is for:** supervisors and managers who must follow the organisation's IP policy and procedures themselves and make sure their teams do.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Know the organisation's requirements
Find and explain the IP policy and procedures, and the roles of the IP officer and legal adviser.
Use other people's IP lawfully
Check licences, get permission in writing, credit sources and keep software licensed.
Protect the organisation's IP
Mark, store and share work and confidential information safely; use non-disclosure agreements and agreements with contractors.
Record and report new IP
Date and keep drafts, report new designs and inventions promptly and keep the IP register up to date.
Respond to breaches
Report suspected misuse or copying with evidence and do not confront or act alone.
Check and improve compliance
Spot-check records, run induction and update procedures when technology changes.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with workplace scenarios and short sums.
A **written paper** with exact terms and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical group tasks**: checking a marketing pack and software records against a policy, and writing a staff IP procedure and delivering an induction briefing.

blocks.note: This unit teaches you the organisation's rules for everyday work. It does not make you a lawyer. When in doubt about whether something is allowed, **ask the IP officer or the legal adviser first**.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Types of intellectual property and who owns it

head: Type
What it protects
How protection arises
Marking or notice
rows: **Copyright**
Written work, software, images, music, video, drawings, training manuals
Automatically when the work is created; no registration needed
Copyright © 2026 Blue Mahoe Training Ltd (the symbol ©, the year and the owner)
**Trade mark**
A brand name, logo, slogan or sign that identifies goods or services
Used in business; stronger when **registered** (in Jamaica with the national intellectual property office, JIPO)
**TM** before registration; **®** only once registered
**Patent**
A new invention
By application and grant, after examination
Patent number or 'patent pending'
**Industrial design**
The appearance of a product (shape, pattern)
By registration
None required
**Trade secret / confidential information**
Formulas, recipes, pricing, client lists, plans that give an advantage and are kept secret
By keeping it secret and controlled
'Confidential' marking, NDAs
**Moral rights**
A creator's right to be named as author and to object to harmful changes
Attach to the creator, even after copyright is sold

ul: A **licence** is permission an owner gives another party to use IP on set terms (what, how many users, for how long, where, for what purpose).
**Attribution** is giving credit to the creator and source.
**Plagiarism** is passing off someone else's written work or ideas as your own.
The **public domain** means a work whose copyright has expired, so anyone may use it.
**Open source** software has published source code under a licence that lets others use and change it, but the licence has conditions.
**Open licences** (such as some image licences) allow reuse, often 'with attribution'.

head: Situation
Usual position
rows: An employee creates work **in the course of her job** (a training manual, a design, a report)
The **employer** usually owns the copyright, unless the contract says otherwise
An employee creates something **outside her job, in her own time**, unrelated to work (a bank clerk writes a cookbook at weekends)
The **employee** usually owns it, unless her contract says otherwise
A **contractor or consultant** creates something
The contractor usually owns it **unless there is a written agreement assigning it**, so sign the agreement first
A client sends you its designs to print
They remain the **client's** IP and confidential, to be used for that job only
Material found on the internet
Most of it is **owned by someone** and needs permission or a licence

blocks.note: In Jamaica, as elsewhere, copyright arises when a work is created: you do not have to register it, although keeping dated copies and records helps you prove ownership. Trade marks, patents and designs are registered through JIPO.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: The law gives owners rights for a limited time. Do not assume that something old is free to use: check whether protection has expired and whether a more recent edition, translation or photograph is protected.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The organisation's IP policy and procedures

blocks.p: An organisation's **IP policy** states what it expects of staff. The **procedures** explain how to do it step by step. A supervisor should know where they are kept, what they say and who to ask. The first place to look when you want to know what the company expects is the **company's IP policy and procedures**.

ul: **Ownership**: who owns work that staff create in their jobs
**Use of others' IP**: rules for software, images, music, fonts, text and video
**Confidentiality**: what is confidential, who may see it and how it is marked and stored
**Recording and reporting** of new IP, and who the IP officer is
**Contractors and suppliers**: agreements before work starts
**Social media and publishing**: what may be posted and when
**Leaving the organisation**: return of files and continuing confidentiality
**Breaches**: how to report them and what happens
Review date and the person responsible

head: Role
Responsibility
rows: Senior management
Approve the policy and provide resources
IP officer (or similar)
Keep the IP register, advise staff, receive reports, deal with registrations and licences
Legal adviser
Advise on difficult cases, contracts and breaches
Supervisor
Explain the rules, make sure the team follows them, report problems
Every employee
Follow the rules, ask when unsure, report new IP and breaches

ul: An **IP register**: its trade marks, designs and other registered or important IP, with dates and owners. It is updated when something changes, such as a new trade mark application being filed.
A **software licence register**: each program, the number of licences, the licence type, the dates and where installed. It shows the organisation uses only what it has paid for.
**Permissions and licences** on file: written permission for each use of someone else's material, setting out the use.
**Confidentiality agreements** and **contractor agreements**.

blocks.p: New staff handling scripts, recordings, client data and designs should learn the IP and confidentiality rules **at induction, before they start the work**, then again at intervals. Include what to do if unsure and who to report to.

blocks.note: Public bodies have additional rules on records and on the use of public resources. Follow the agency's own policy as well as the general rules.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Using other people's intellectual property lawfully

blocks.p: The basic rule: **use someone else's work only if you own a licence, have written permission, or the law or an open licence clearly allows it.** The fact that something is on the internet does not make it free.

head: Material
The usual requirement
What to do
rows: Software
A licence for each user or device, as the licence says
Install only approved, licensed programs. Keep a register. Do not copy programs or install 'personal use only' software on work machines.
Fonts
Licence terms often differ for personal and business or commercial use
Check that the licence allows business use before using it in client work
Photographs and images
Copyright usually belongs to the photographer or agency
Use your own, buy a licence, use images licensed for your purpose, or get written permission. Credit the creator if the licence requires attribution
Music
Playing recorded music in public (a restaurant, hotel lobby, shop) usually needs a licence from the music licensing body
Hold the licence; use music cleared for your video or event
Video clips and films
Copyright owner's permission or licence
Check the licence or get permission before showing a clip in training or marketing
Published text and reports
Short extracts may be quoted with credit; copying large parts needs permission
Quote briefly and name the source; do not copy whole pages
Photocopying or scanning books
Limited by law and licence
Check the licence; buy copies or get permission for the whole class
Logos and brands of other firms
They are trade marks
Use them only with the owner's permission, never to suggest approval you do not have
Open-source code
Licence conditions apply (for example sharing changes, or giving credit)
Check the licence terms with the IP officer **before** adding it to a product you will sell
Another firm's confidential information
It must not be used if it was obtained wrongly
Stop using it and report it properly

blocks.p: A program is licensed for 20 users but is found on 26 computers. The shortfall is 26 − 20 = 6. The organisation must **remove 6 copies or buy 6 more licences**. If each extra licence costs J$18,000, the cost is 6 × 18,000 = J$108,000. If a program is needed by 35 staff and each licence covers 5 users, the organisation needs 35 ÷ 5 = 7 licences.
A planned check of an organisation's computers to confirm that every program is properly licensed is an **audit**. Run one regularly, and fix gaps at once.

ul: Put quotes in quotation marks and give the source.
Say where an image came from.
Do not copy a competitor's website text into your proposal: write your own and cite sources for facts.
Keep **written permission** on file for each use of another firm's photographs or text, stating what use is allowed.

blocks.note: A licence for 'internal use only' does not allow you to sell or give an adapted version to clients. If you want to use work beyond the licence, get the owner's agreement first.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: A music licence for a restaurant or hotel lobby is usually bought from the licensing body for composers and publishers in Jamaica. Ask the IP officer or the legal adviser who holds the organisation's licences.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Protecting the organisation's own IP and confidential information

ul: Mark documents 'Confidential' when they are, such as tender prices sent to a partner under an NDA.
Use the copyright notice on manuals, courses, reports and websites: © year and owner.
Use **TM** for a brand that is not yet registered, **®** only when it is.
Keep confidential files in locked storage or restricted folders, with access limited to those who need them (the 'need to know' rule).
Follow a **clear desk** rule: put papers away and clear your desk when you are not there.
Do not store confidential material on personal devices or accounts.

head: Agreement
Purpose
Typical use
rows: **Non-disclosure agreement (NDA)**
Stops the other person sharing what they learn
Visitors to a factory; partners receiving tender prices; consultants
Contractor agreement with IP clause
Makes clear who owns the work and requires confidentiality
A contractor building an app or writing training videos
Employment contract
Ownership of work done in the job, confidentiality, return of property
All staff
Licence agreement
Sets the terms on which the organisation lets another party use its IP
Training materials licensed to a client

blocks.p: Before a contractor starts building an app or a training course, the manager should check that an **agreement on IP ownership and confidentiality** is signed.

ul: Staff should not post photos, details or prototypes of products before they are **approved for release**.
Before speaking at an event, say only what has **already been made public**.
Check with marketing or the IP officer before releasing designs, formulas or client work.
Do not post other people's material without permission.
Ask visitors to sign an NDA where they will see confidential processes.
Treat a client's unreleased designs as the **client's confidential IP for that job only**.
Do not share one client's work with another.
Collect all files, devices, keys and access.
Remind the person of continuing confidentiality.
Remove access promptly.
Do not let departing staff take client lists or designs.

blocks.h: New staff and other firms' secrets

blocks.p: A new staff member must not bring or use a **former employer's** or a competitor's confidential information. If she admits that she has, her supervisor should stop its use and report it properly, so that the organisation does not become involved in misuse of another firm's secrets.

blocks.note: Confidentiality is not only about papers. Conversations in public places, whiteboards left uncleaned after a meeting and screens visible to visitors can all give secrets away.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Recording, reporting and dealing with breaches

blocks.p: Staff who create something new (a design, a recipe, a process, software, a training course) should follow the reporting procedure. The reasons:

ul: To **prove ownership and the date of creation**: keep dated drafts and a record of who created what.
To allow **protection to be sought before disclosure**: a design or invention shown to the public first may lose protection.
To keep the IP register accurate and complete.
To let the organisation use and license it properly.

flow: Create and date the work, keeping drafts and notes
Store it securely, with a record of who created it
Report it promptly to the IP officer, on the form or system
The IP officer records it in the register and decides on protection (copyright notice, trade mark, design or patent application, trade secret)
Update the register when something changes

blocks.p: A new brand name should be searched and cleared before use, and a new trade mark application is entered in the register when it is filed. Registered trade marks have to be renewed after a fixed period set by the law, so the register should show the **renewal dates**.

blocks.note: An employee who developed something on her own before joining the firm should **declare it**, so that it is recorded as hers and there is no later dispute.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A breach is when IP is used or shared without permission or in breach of a licence. It may be an outsider copying your material, an insider misusing it, or your own team using someone else's. Report promptly, because **delay can weaken the organisation's position** and let the harm spread.

flow: Stop and do not confront the person yourself
Record what you saw: date, place, web address, screenshots
Report to the IP officer (or the person named in the procedure)
Keep the evidence safe and the matter confidential
Let the IP officer and legal adviser decide the action (a letter, a take-down request, discipline, legal action)
Help to put right what caused it, such as a gap in training or access

ul: A seller offering copies of your paid training videos online: report to the IP officer **with screenshots**.
A former employee using your firm's client training materials in his new business: report; do not confront or accuse.
A slogan your team created that may be close to a rival's registered trade mark: ask the IP officer or legal adviser **before** using it.

head: Reason
Effect of ignoring the rules
rows: Legal
Legal claims, orders to stop and damages
Financial
Costs of settlement, buying licences late, lost value of unprotected ideas
Reputation
Harm to the organisation's name and to client trust
People
Disciplinary action against the staff concerned

ul: **Spot-check** work and licence records regularly: compare installed software with the register; check images and music in marketing items against permissions on file.

Check that new IP is logged. For example, if a design team has 150 designs this year and the procedure requires each to be logged, and 114 are logged, then 114 ÷ 150 × 100 = **76%** are logged and 36 are missing.
Ask staff about problems without blame so that issues come out early.
Record findings and corrective actions, with owners and dates.

blocks.p: A procedure written before staff began using **AI writing tools and cloud storage** will not cover them. The supervisor should **raise the gap** so that the procedure can be updated. In the meantime, ask before putting confidential or client material into any online tool, and check the licence terms of images and text from AI tools.

blocks.h: Handling a shortfall found in an audit

flow: Confirm the facts from the register and the machines
Remove unlicensed copies or buy the missing licences
Tell your manager and the IP officer
Find the cause (who could install, who approved)
Fix the cause (restrict installation rights, central purchasing, training)
Record the correction and re-check later

blocks.p: In a public agency, buying extra licences is also a purchase and must follow the agency's procurement rules.

ul: Review the policy on its review date and when technology or the law changes.
Update induction and quizzes with real examples from your workplace.
Share lessons from breaches or near misses.
Use a short quiz at induction to check understanding.

blocks.note: An organisation that respects other people's IP is respected in return. Staff who are shown how to use material lawfully are less likely to make a mistake that costs the organisation money and trust.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: name the main types of IP (copyright, trade marks, patents, designs, trade secrets) and the marks © , TM and ®
say who usually owns work created by employees, contractors and outside work
find and explain my organisation's IP policy and procedures and the IP officer's role
check licences and get written permission before using software, fonts, images, music, video and text
count licences and work out the cost of a shortfall
quote and credit sources properly and avoid plagiarism
protect confidential information with marking, storage, clear desk and non-disclosure agreements
make sure contractors sign an IP and confidentiality agreement before work starts
record new IP, keep dated drafts and report it to the IP officer promptly
report suspected breaches with evidence and without confronting anyone
spot-check compliance and raise gaps when technology changes
run an induction on IP and confidentiality for new staff

terms: Creations of the mind that the law protects: writing, designs, brands, software, inventions, secrets.
The right of a creator over written work, music, images, software and similar works; arises automatically.
A brand name, logo or slogan that identifies a business; TM before registration, ® after.
Confidential information that gives an advantage and is kept secret.
A creator's right to be named and to object to harmful changes.
Permission to use IP on set terms.
Giving credit to the creator and the source.
Passing off someone else's work as your own.
Works whose copyright has expired, which anyone may use.
Software whose code is published under a licence that allows use and change.
An agreement not to share confidential information.
The organisation's record of its IP.
A planned check, such as of software licences.
The rule to put papers away when you leave your desk.
The Jamaica Intellectual Property Office, which registers trade marks, patents and designs.

c1.title: Licensing a design program at a Kingston community college
c1.text: A community college in Kingston has 38 computers with a computer-aided design program installed, but only 30 user licences. Each extra licence costs J$18,500. The college's IT officer found the problem during a routine check. Any staff member with an administrator password can install software on the lab computers, and there is no licence register.

c2.title: A tour operator's brochure and video in Ocho Rios
c2.text: A tour operator in Ocho Rios is preparing a new brochure and a promotional video. A designer has taken a photograph from a travel website, used a font downloaded from a free font site, and added the logo of a partner hotel. The video uses a popular reggae song as background music. The brochure also quotes two paragraphs from a published tourism research report. The operator's policy requires permissions to be kept on file.

c3.title: A new sauce at a Mandeville food processor
c3.text: A food processor in Mandeville has developed a new pepper sauce. Shanice, a product developer employed by the firm, created the recipe at work. The firm has chosen a brand name for the sauce but has only just applied to register it. It has also hired a freelance designer to create the label and a freelance video producer to make a training film. No written agreement has been signed with either freelancer. A visitor group will tour the factory next week.

c4.title: Misuse of course materials at a Savanna-la-Mar training institute
c4.text: A training institute in Savanna-la-Mar has written its own course manuals and videos. The institute's receptionist tells the manager that a former instructor, who left four months ago, is advertising courses on social media that look like copies of the institute's slides. The manager also finds, during an exit check, that another leaving instructor has copied files onto a personal flash drive.

c5.title: A design unit's records at a Kingston advertising agency
c5.text: The design unit of a Kingston advertising agency produced 150 designs this year, and its procedure requires each to be logged in the IP register. Only 114 are logged. A junior designer copied three paragraphs from a competitor's website into a client proposal. The procedure was written before the agency began using online storage for client files.

questions.q: How much will it cost the college to licence the extra copies?
questions.why: Shortfall = 38 − 30 = 8 copies. Cost = 8 × J$18,500 = J$148,000. J$703,000 would be all 38 copies at the full price.

questions.q: What should the college do about the 8 unlicensed copies?
o: Remove 8 copies or buy 8 more licences
Leave them until a customer complains
Buy 4 licences and share them across 8 computers
Move the program to another lab
questions.why: An organisation may use software only as far as it is licensed. The fix is to match licences to use, by removing copies or buying licences. Sharing licences beyond their terms is still a breach.

questions.q: Which action best stops the problem recurring?
o: Ask students and staff not to install anything
Delete the design software from every computer
Buy a licence for every computer in the college
Limit installation rights and keep a register
questions.why: The cause is that anyone with a password can install software, and there is no record of licences. Limiting rights and keeping a register give control. Buying for every computer is expensive and does not prevent unlicensed copies.

questions.q: The college decides to buy the extra licences. As a public body, what must it also do?
o: Pay the supplier in cash to save time
Follow its procurement rules in the purchase
Ask staff to buy them personally
Wait until the next financial year
questions.why: Buying licences is a purchase of goods or services and a public body must follow its procurement rules. Delay leaves the breach in place.

questions.q: What must the designer check before using the photograph from the travel website?
o: That it appears on the first page of search results
That she has a licence or written permission to use it
That it has no visible watermark
That the website is well known
questions.why: A photograph is protected by copyright. Being on the internet does not make it free. Written permission or a licence that covers the use is required.

questions.q: What is the main concern about the font from the free font site?
o: Fonts cannot be used in brochures
Free fonts are always low quality
Fonts need to be registered at JIPO
Its licence may not cover business use
questions.why: Free fonts often come with licences for personal use only. The designer should check that the licence allows business use before using it in client work.

questions.q: What is the correct approach to the reggae song in the video?
o: Get a licence or permission, or use cleared music
Use it, because the video is only a minute long
Use it, but keep the volume low under the voiceover
Use it, because tourists will enjoy it so much
questions.why: Recorded music is protected by copyright, and its use in a promotional video needs a licence or permission from the rights owners. Short length or low volume does not remove the need.

questions.q: How should the operator use the two paragraphs from the research report?
o: Copy them in full and leave out the author
Change a few words and use them as its own work
Quote briefly and credit the source clearly
Use them freely, because the report is out of print
questions.why: A short quote with credit is the usual accepted practice, as long as it follows the policy. Leaving out the source or passing the text off as your own is plagiarism.

questions.q: Which evidence should the operator keep on file for the partner hotel's logo?
o: A screenshot of the hotel's website
The designer's note that the hotel is a friend
Written permission setting out the use
A copy of the brochure
questions.why: A logo is a trade mark. Written permission that describes the use proves the operator is allowed to use it and stops any later dispute.

questions.q: How is the pepper sauce recipe most likely to be protected?
o: As a trade secret, with controlled access
By registering the recipe as a trade mark
By putting the copyright symbol on the bottle
By publishing it on the firm's website
questions.why: A recipe is valuable because it is secret, so it is protected by restricted access, confidentiality agreements and careful handling. A trade mark protects a brand, not a recipe.

questions.q: Which mark should the firm use beside the brand name while the registration is pending?
o: None until registration is complete
TM
questions.why: TM is used to claim a mark before registration. ® may be used only once the mark is registered, and © relates to copyright.

questions.q: What is the main risk of letting the freelancers work with no signed agreement?
o: The work will end up costing more than planned
The freelancers may own the work they create
The freelancers may not finish the work on time
The firm cannot use the work anywhere in Jamaica
questions.why: Without a written agreement assigning ownership, the person who creates the work usually owns the copyright. An agreement on ownership and confidentiality should be signed before work starts.

questions.q: What should the firm do about the factory tour?
o: Ban cameras and rely on visitors' good manners
Have visitors sign a non-disclosure agreement
Show only the packing area, not the kitchen
Let visitors in with a staff escort only
questions.why: An NDA creates a legal duty not to share what visitors see or hear. Camera rules help but do not replace it.

questions.q: What should the manager do about the former instructor's adverts?
o: Telephone the former instructor and accuse him of theft
Post a warning about him on social media
Ignore it, because he no longer works there
Report to the IP officer and keep evidence such as screenshots
questions.why: The IP officer and legal adviser decide the action. Evidence with dates and web addresses is needed, and the manager should not confront or accuse the person herself.

questions.q: Why should the manager report promptly?
o: Delay can weaken its position and let harm spread
Reports are only accepted within seven days
The IP officer will otherwise be disciplined
The former instructor may leave the country
questions.why: Late action may let the copying grow and weaken the institute's ability to stop it or claim for losses. Prompt action also helps preserve evidence.

questions.q: What is the best response to the instructor who copied files to a personal flash drive?
o: Let him keep them, since he created some of them
Ask him to keep the files safe and private
Follow the exit procedure and recover the files
Take no action unless a client complains later
questions.why: The exit procedure should return all files and remind leavers of continuing confidentiality. Material produced in his job belongs to the institute.

questions.q: Which step in the institute's induction would have reduced such risks?
o: Giving staff a free copy of all course materials
Telling staff about the rules on their last day only
Teaching confidentiality and file rules before staff start
Asking staff to read the rules in their own time
questions.why: Rules on confidentiality and file handling should be taught at induction, before staff start work, and repeated, so they know what is expected well before they leave.

questions.q: What percentage of the designs has been logged?
questions.why: 114 ÷ 150 × 100 = 76%. 36 designs are missing from the register.

questions.q: What should the supervisor do about the paragraphs copied from the competitor's website?
o: Leave them in, because the proposal is private
Change a few words so they look different
Ask the client whether it minds the copying
Rewrite in the firm's own words and credit the facts
questions.why: Copying another firm's text is plagiarism and may breach its copyright. The proposal should contain the firm's own words, with sources credited for facts.

questions.q: The procedure was written before online storage was used for client files. What should the supervisor do?
o: Do nothing until a problem occurs
Raise it so that the procedure can be updated
Stop using the online storage at once
Ask clients to take responsibility for their files
questions.why: Procedures should be reviewed when technology changes. Raising the gap lets the organisation add rules on access, location and client confidentiality without stopping useful tools.
